call_verification.baseline:
Measured on this Mac on 2026-09-24: fresh worktree, RelWithDebInfo, unity build, no ccache.
- Clean `build.sh release --make`: 314 s for 324 C++ units plus 40 C units. That is about 8 s configure and 306 s make, roughly 7,450 lines/s overall.
- No-op rebuild: 1 s.
- One edited .cpp outside a unity group: 9 s.
- One edited file inside a unity group: 37 s. That is 32 s to compile the 46,590-line group, 3.5 s to archive, and about 1.2 s to relink the 193 MB binary.
- Rust: `cargo check` on the workspace 7 s; `cargo build --release -p sql-nio` 17 s. Inside the C++ build, the sql-nio release step takes 38.6 s and a second cargo build of jemalloc takes 54 s.

CI (32 cores, ccache):
- Compile step median 223 s; a true cold cache takes 556 s of make plus 258 s of dependency init.
- The four mysqltest slices have medians of 574, 374, 447 and 370 s, about 29 min of serial test time for 272 cases.
- A successful run takes about 19 min wall time.

Local judge time: about 27 min for the configured set, but that figure comes only from seekdb-dev notes. The run records they cite are gone, so it is unverified.

This is the cost of feedback today:
- 9-37 s per edit;
- about 5 min per clean build;
- about 30 min per full judge run.
call_verification.rust_scaling_assumption:
All of these are assumptions unless marked otherwise.

(1) Size. About 2.28M hand-written C++ lines are translation work (2,314,419 minus rust/sql-nio 8,448 minus the 24,585 grammar lines), less roughly 65K kept in C++ islands. That becomes about 1.8-2.9M Rust lines, a 0.8-1.3x ratio. Headers are 26% of src and are not duplicated in Rust. Bun's Zig-to-Rust ratio was 1.46x.

(2) Check speed. cargo check runs at 500-5,000 lines/s per M4 core, central about 2,500. This is the verifier's corrected range from TiKV clippy (about 95 s for about 0.73M lines on 3 vCPUs) and GreptimeDB (425-886 s with warm dependencies). The single-crate frontend is serial on stable Rust; -Zthreads is nightly only.

(3) Crate layout. 20-40 crates of at most about 100-150K lines each, in a 5-8 level chain, seeded from the Bazel graph that is already acyclic at the header level: src/sql/sql_runtime_group_deps.bzl, 79 oblib and 116 share interface targets.

(4) Machine limits:
- Cargo holds a lock on its build directory, so parallel agents cannot each run cargo against one target directory (general Cargo behavior).
- A target directory for about 2.5M lines with debug info is assumed to need 20-60 GB, against 52 GiB free.
- rustc on a 100-150K-line crate is assumed to need 2-8 GiB, so 24 GiB allows only 2-4 large checks at once.

(5) Release profile. The current [profile.release] (codegen-units=1, lto=thin) serializes LLVM per crate. Databend took 30m37s even with 99% sccache hits because of one ~181K-line crate. Feldera took about 25 min for 100K lines in one crate. So the dev loop needs codegen-units of 16 or more and no LTO.
call_verification.estimate:
Referee prices, with where each sits in the loop:

1. Per crate (leaf-crate check, `cargo check -p`): 100-150K lines at 500-5,000 lines/s is about 20 s-5 min, central about 40-60 s. It runs from a single build daemon (scripts/build_daemon.sh) whenever a crate's batch of units lands, not inside each unit's loop.

2. After an edit to a foundation crate (the oblib/share equivalents), every downstream crate is re-checked: about 2-4 min central, 15-30 min pessimistic. This hits every Step 4 fixer wave that touches shared types.

3. Clean workspace check: about 1.5-3 min optimistic, about 3-5 min central (2.5M lines at 2,500 lines/s with about 5 effective parallel crates), about 20-30 min pessimistic. It runs once per Step 4 round, for an assumed 20-80 rounds: roughly 1-40 hours of daemon time in total.

4. Rejected alternative, one 1.83M-line crate: 6-60 min per clean check, incremental time unknown. Too slow for any loop.

5. Dev-profile build of the whole Rust tree plus a link with the islands: assumption 10-40 min clean, a few minutes incremental. Release with today's profile would take hours. This runs once per Step 5 iteration.

6. Full judge on this Mac: 272 cases take about 27-30 min serial. Running 4 slices in parallel on separate ports should take about 8-12 min, if 4 server instances fit in 24 GiB (assumption). The C++ side of a differential run is recorded once at a frozen commit, so each run pays only the Rust side. With the corpora and scenarios the judge needs to add (see call_tests), a full run is assumed to take 30-90 min. It runs nightly and at gates. In Step 6, each fix re-runs only its failing cases (seconds to minutes).

Compared with C++ today (9-37 s per edit, 314 s clean), Rust is about 2-10x more expensive per full-graph check but similar per leaf crate.

Therefore Step 4 does not fold into Step 3 across the board:
- 4,000 units would contend for one cargo lock, about 50 GB of disk and 24 GiB of RAM.
- Foundation crates cascade.
Step 3 stays compiler-free per unit. The daemon checks each crate as its batch completes, which partly folds Step 4 in for leaf crates only. The full survey build runs in rounds.

The disk limit comes first: free at least about 150 GB, or add an external SSD, before Step 4 (assumption).

call_tests.build_judge_first:
Run prompts/00b-judge-setup.md before Step 1 with these tasks. Costs are bands and assumptions.

1. Local runner.
   - Commit the --nodaemon call in mysqltest_for_seekdb.py (a one-line change, since sdb.py already accepts the flag).
   - Pin the case order and slice count, and add a no-retry mode.
   - Run the 272 cases on a frozen C++ commit and record the pass list.
   Cost: 1-2 days wall, about 30 min per run, 2-4 h attention.

2. One-day coverage run.
   - Re-enable WITH_COVERAGE (the guard at CMakeLists.txt:147) or pass -fprofile-instr-generate / -fcoverage-mapping.
   - Run the 272 cases, then llvm-cov per function, and map the result to the 52 unit groups.
   This sizes everything below.

3. Differential mode.
   - Run the frozen C++ build once, store its outputs, and diff each candidate against them.
   - Optional normalizers: mask EST.ROWS/EST.TIME in the 40 plan files; sort unordered rows per case. They are only needed where Call 1 lets output drift.
   - Validate: C++ against C++ must give 0 diffs, and hand-made mutations must each fail (flip a comparison in an ob_expr_*.cpp, change an errno, drop a filter).

4. Generated corpora, recorded on C++:
   - one SELECT per expression name over a type matrix, covering the 320 unreached names;
   - a DDL/DCL statement per unreached resolver;
   - hint-forced plans for the unreached operators and rewrite rules.
   Cost: about 5,000-20,000 statements, 0.2-4B processed tokens, 2-4 weeks wall.

5. Restart and replay: an sdb.py start → load → stop (kill) → start script on the same base-dir, then compare a fixed SELECT set.

6. Binary protocol: replay the 272 cases with mysqltest --ps-protocol and diff C++ against the candidate.

7. Embedded: fix the bindings socket paths (4 of the 12 cases build 104-107-character paths, which macOS rejects at 104 bytes), then run the 12 gtests and 7 seekdb-async tests against each binary.

8. Concurrency and performance baselines:
   - 4 parallel slices on separate ports;
   - run_two_concurrent_clients.sh in a loop;
   - sysbench oltp_point_select and oltp_read_write at 1/16/64 threads in Docker;
   - start and restart times from seekdb.log.

9. wasm, only if in scope: drive the 272 cases through tools/wasm/mysqltest-bridge.mjs on the branch, and automate database-browser.html in headless Chrome.

10. A tiered init: a minimal init without the PL procedure or set_tp, so the 130 plain-SQL cases can judge a Rust server before PL and the tracepoint registry exist.

Total: 3-6 weeks wall, about 0.3-5B processed tokens, 30-60 h of developer attention. All of it is useful for the C++ code even if the port never happens.
parity_scenarios: Plain-SQL tier: the 130 cases that need no OB internals, run under a minimal init, diffed against recorded C++ output (for example t/join_basic.test).
Full-gate tier: all 272 configured cases after tools/deploy/init.sql and init_user.sql, fixed order, no retries, 4 slices on separate ports.

Plan parity: the 40 plan-bearing configured .result files (658 tables, 568 with EST.ROWS/EST.TIME), exact at first, with an opt-in cost mask (for example test_suite/executor/r/mysql/basic.result, 152 tables).

Expression and cast matrix: SELECT f(args) for all 527 registered expression names over int, decimal, double, string, date, JSON and NULL inputs, recorded on C++, including error codes and warnings (320 names reach no test today).
Arithmetic formatting: datatype/div, t/add, datatype/minus and expr/mul (770,711 expected lines), which pin ObNumber and dtoa output.

Restart and replay: start, load rows with obclient, kill (SIGTERM is turned into SIGKILL by ob_signal_handle.cpp:129-134), start on the same base-dir, compare a fixed SELECT set. Seeded from bindings ChangedMemoryLimitSurvivesRestart and async conn_open_shares_one_handle_per_dir.
Binary protocol: the 272 cases replayed with mysqltest --ps-protocol, diffed C++ against Rust (rust/sql-nio/src/command.rs:43-49 has no judge today).

Embedded process contract: the 12 seekdb-bindings gtests (after the socket-path fix) and the 7 seekdb-async tests, checking argv flags, run/sql.sock, the run/seekdb.clients flock, the store/sstable first-start probe and root@sys.
Concurrency: 69 configured cases open extra connections and 6 use send/reap. Add run_two_concurrent_clients.sh in a loop and sysbench at 16/64 threads.
Performance gate: sysbench QPS and latency, cold start and restart time, full judge wall time, as ratios against a C++ baseline recorded on this Mac.
Derived-data behavior: the 42 geometry, 22 vector_index and 15 fts_index suites, checked through query results (S2 coverings, vsag snapshots and IK tokens must match in behavior, not in bytes).
Cutover: a logical export from the C++ v1.4.0 binary (SELECT INTO OUTFILE / mysqldump) imported into the Rust build for every column type and index kind. Today 0 OUTFILE and 0 mysqldump tests exist.

strategy.sequencing:
Phase A, weeks 0-6. First usable results.
- The developer makes the product decisions listed under decisions.
- Run the 00b judge work (useful for the C++ today).
- Time `cargo check` on an existing 150-200K-line Rust crate on this Mac to pin the check rate and memory use.
- Free disk.

Phase B, weeks 4-16. Step 1.
- The design document replaces the rulebook.
- scripts/depmap_c.py is adapted to key units by class, not path, because 73 api headers and 118 forwarders put declarations and code in different directories. It is condensed to a 20-40 crate plan seeded from the Bazel group maps.
- Gap inventory at field and class granularity.
- Hand-built substrate crates.
- The second usable result: a parity-tested Rust value library (ObNumber, time conversion, charset, JSON, casts).

Phase C. Step 2.
- Pilot on the nastiest stems.
- One disposable run over the core-adjacent groups, about 500 units, replaces the bakeoff.

Phase D. Step 3, leaves to root, with the daemon checking each crate as it fills:
1. oblib
2. share, logservice, tx and storage
3. sql
4. observer, rootserver and pl

Phase E. Step 4 rounds to zero errors.

Phase F. Step 5.
- Boot with the tiered init: plain-SQL cases first, then the full init.sql.
- About 10% of the code (vector and retrieval, standby, AI functions, jobs, DBMS_STATS, parts of the virtual tables, XML) can be ordered last to shorten time to first boot.

Phase G. Step 6 burn-down, then prompts/06-post-parity.md.

What this sequencing cannot change: the first end-to-end SQL signal from the Rust tree arrives only after about 90% of the code is translated and compiling. Bootstrap needs schema loading through inner SQL, the generated inner tables and the PL resolvers for system packages. Everything before that point is judged only by reviewers, the compiler and library-level parity tests.

alternatives.name: Translate everything structure-preserving into a parallel tree, then switch (the kit's default path)
Replace parts inside the running binary behind an FFI boundary, one module at a time
alternatives.why_not:
Cost of the seams:
- sql + storage + query + data_plane + pl (about 1.83M lines) share ObExpr, ObEvalCtx and filter executors in the scan path (ob_tablet_scan.h; 1,069 sql:: lines in 98 storage files), so the largest group cannot be split without first redesigning that boundary.
- Base classes are subclassed across modules (ObTimerTask 72, ObDLinkBase 72, ObFuncExprOperator 313), so each needs a vtable bridge.
- Header-only containers (ObIArray, 290 uses in the api headers) cannot cross a C ABI.
- Mixed releases need byte-identical slog, clog and sstable codecs.
- Only one Rust staticlib can be linked.
- Each seam costs about 2% unsafe, as in sql-nio (186 in 8,448 lines).
Its one advantage is that the judge works from day one. That covers at most the periphery (logservice 32.7K, standby 14.9K, parser), about 10% of the code, and the bridges are thrown away later. The developer already discarded a plan of this shape.

alternatives.name: Keep large C++ islands for good (for example keep storage or the whole SQL engine in C++)
alternatives.why_not: The scan and filter boundary between sql and storage is SQL engine code compiled inline into storage. ObExpr::eval is OB_INLINE at ob_expr.h:1039, and storage calls locate_datum_for_write 28 times. A permanent split needs identical #[repr(C)] layouts on both sides or a redesigned filter interface, which is the same redesign cost without removing the C++. Islands are worth it only where a third-party C++ library forces them (vsag, S2, boost.geometry, ICU).

alternatives.name: Clean-room rewrite of a new Rust database that speaks the same protocol
Don't migrate; harden the C++ instead
alternatives.why_not: This is the fallback if the verdict's single fact comes back low. It costs far less: an ASan/TSan CI job, NDEBUG-independent bounds checks, and the 00b judge work, which is needed anyway. It does not remove the refactor-risk pattern, where memory bugs follow each large ownership refactor, and it does not fit the product direction that is already adding Rust (sql-nio, the 34.6K-line feature/plugin runtime, feature/rust). Not rejected outright; kept as the result if the coverage check fails.

positions.six_steps:
The kit's six steps, one line each:
1. Create the map and the rules: dependency map, gap inventory, rulebook.
2. Stress-test the rules: bakeoff plus a pilot.
3. Translate everything: implementer, two adversarial reviewers and a fixer per unit, fanned out over a disk queue.
4. Compile: one survey build turns errors into a sliced queue for fixers with no compiler access.
5. Run it: hello world, then smoke tests.
6. Match behavior: burn down the judge's failures against the old code.

Instantiated for seekdb (worktree /Users/colin/seekdb-dev/migrate-to-rust, HEAD 076eb309b). Wall and attention figures are bands and assumptions.

**Pre-Step 1, the judge: prompts/00b-judge-setup.md.**
- Work: see call_tests build_judge_first.
- Units: 272 cases, plus about 5,000-20,000 generated corpus statements, plus 6 scenario families.
- Wall 3-6 weeks; attention 30-60 h.

**Step 1a, the design document in place of a rulebook (templates/RULEBOOK.md used as a design doc).**
It must decide:
- the OOM policy: abort, plus typed checks at the 8 named budget owners (clog, replay, IO allocator, KV cache store, vector module, query memory tracker, memstore-full check, temp-file write buffer pool), plus the logical -4013 errors;
- arena lifetimes against owned values for ObString (17,716 mentions) and ObIAllocator (2,498 files);
- the error type, including about 6,000 error-as-outcome sites;
- context passing (1,222 server_service lines over 122 types);
- retyping about 823 ATOMIC_* field names;
- an enum-or-trait rule for 4,626 derived classes;
- derive macros for OB_UNIS (only if compatibility is kept, which is not recommended) and TO_STRING_KV;
- stacker for 1,138 SMART_CALL sites;
- sort and hash determinism;
- the 20-40 crate plan;
- the five island ABIs.
Wall 6-16 weeks; attention 120-300 h. This is the long pole and cannot be delegated.

**Step 1b, the dependency map: prompts/01-dependency-map.md with an adapted scripts/depmap_c.py.**
- Units: 6,468 hand-written files, keyed by class.
- It must resolve the 118 forwarding headers and the unity-hidden includes, and check crate-level cycles: at directory level there is one 110-directory, 4,108-file cycle, and 4 include lines tie sql, storage and rootserver together.
- The closing make_manifest.py step produces about 4,000-4,200 units from 3,692 stems capped at 20-30K tokens, after splitting the 54 hand-written files of 4K lines or more (ob_ddl_service.cpp 23,564 lines, ob_join_order.cpp 17,680, ...).
- Wall 3-7 days; attention 4-8 h.

**Step 1c, the gap inventory: prompts/02-gap-inventory.md, gap = ownership and lifetimes.**
- Sweep at field and class granularity rather than every call site: 5,938 raw-pointer fields, 130 Handle classes, 441 inc/dec_ref lines, 1,733 const_cast lines, 3,824 reinterpret_cast lines, 2,741 placement-new lines.
- Expect about 6,000-12,000 rows.
- Wall 2-4 weeks; attention 15-30 h, mostly UNKNOWN rows.

**Step 2, stress test: prompts/03-stress-test.md, pilot half only.**
- The bakeoff is invalid for a redesign. Replace it with adversarial review of the design doc plus one disposable run over about 500 core-adjacent units (oblib-types, share-types-datum, a slice of sql-expr), at the implementer tier with no reviewers, then thrown away.
- Pilot on the highest-scoring stems: ob_raw_expr, ob_tx_ctx, ob_tablet, ob_chunk_datum_store.
- Wall 2-4 weeks; attention 20-40 h.

**Step 3, translate: prompts/04-translation-kickoff.md with scripts/queue_runner.mjs over migration/manifest.tsv, batches of 100.**
- About 4,000 units across 52 unit groups, in crate order.
- Excluded from translation: data (the IK dictionary, 276,043 lines, becomes a resource file by script; the tz tables), generated code (retarget the 6 generators: gen_errno.pl, gen_ob_sys_variables.py, generate_inner_table_schema.py, syspack_codegen.py, gen_str_datum_func_parts.py, gen_expr_str_cmp_func.py), vendored code (zstd, xxhash, libeasy → crates), dead code (30,874 lines plus lib/codec, which is compiled but unused), and the islands.
- templates/settings.json must be installed first.
- Wall 2-6 weeks at 40-80 concurrent agents (rate limits unknown); attention 20-40 h over about 40 batch gates plus amendments.

**Step 4, compile: prompts/05-survey-build.md with scripts/build_daemon.sh --cmd 'cargo check --workspace --message-format=short'.**
- The daemon also checks each crate as its batch lands.
- Errors assumed 20K-150K; Bun's rate was about 16,000 errors for about 780K Rust lines.
- 20-80 rounds.
- Wall 2-6 weeks; attention 20-60 h.
- Not dissolved into Step 3 (see call_verification).

**Step 5, run it (no kit prompt).**
- Hello world: the Rust server bootstraps (generated inner tables, sysvars, errno, system packages through the PL resolvers) and answers `select 1` through obclient.
- Then the tiered init and the 130 plain-SQL cases, then the full init.sql and the 272 cases.
- Wall 3-10 weeks; attention 80-250 h. The attention peak falls here, on one person.

**Step 6, match behavior: the 00b judge.**
- Triage every failure by running it on the frozen C++: regression, inherited or environment.
- Burn down 272 cases plus the corpora plus the restart, PS-protocol, embedded and performance scenarios.
- Then prompts/06-post-parity.md for the BUG(port), TODO(port) and PERF(port) markers.
- Wall 6-20 weeks; attention 80-250 h.

**Totals: about 6-18 months of calendar time and about 400-1,100 hours of developer attention.**
positions.cost_bands:
All figures are bands, not predictions.

**Units and prices**
- Units: about 4,000 translation units (3,692 hand-written stems, median 2.6K tokens, mean 6.6K; one-level include context median 25.6K, mean about 35K; total 24.26M code tokens).
- Review topology per unit: implementer + 2 reviewers + fixer, plus an arbiter on about 20% of units.
- "Processed tokens" means all input including cache reads, plus output. Agent loops re-read context on every turn, so this is 10-100x the code size.
- The survey calibration (43 subagents, 8.92M tokens, 117 min) likely does not count cache re-reads. I use it only as a throughput check, not as a per-token price.
- Prices from the claude-api skill:
  - Sonnet 5: $2/$10, cache reads $0.20 per M tokens.
  - Opus 5.5: $4/$20, cache reads $0.20.
  - Fable 5.1: $10/$50, cache reads $0.25.
  - Cache writes cost 1.25x input. Batch API is 50% off, but it does not apply to agent loops.
- Blended cost per M processed tokens (Sonnet 5 as implementer and fixer, Opus 5.5 as reviewers): about $0.57 with 92% cache reads, about $1.40 with 70% cache reads (assumption).

**Step 3 (translate)**
- Per unit: implementer 0.9-6M + 2 reviewers × 0.6-3M + fixer 0.3-1.5M + arbiter about 0.1M = about 2.5-14M processed tokens.
- × 4,000 units = about 10-55B processed tokens.
- × $0.57-1.40 per M = about $6K-80K.

**Step 4 (compile)**
- 20K-150K errors (assumption) ÷ 20-50 per slice = 400-7,500 slices.
- × (fixer 1-4M + 2 reviewers 0.5-2M) = about 1-30B processed tokens, about $1K-40K.
- Plus 20-80 check rounds × 3-30 min on the local daemon.

**Step 1 (map and rules)**
- Design by Fable 5.1 with the developer: 50-200 long sessions × 2-10M = 0.1-2B, at about $1.6-4.5 per M = about $0.2K-9K.
- Gap inventory: 300-600 batches × 3 agents × 1-4M = 1-7B, about $1K-10K.
- Dependency map: under 0.1B.

**Step 2 (stress test)**
- Pilot plus 1-2 disposable runs of about 500 units × 1-6M = 0.5-6B, about $0.3K-8K.

**Judge first (00b)**
- 0.3-5B, about $0.2K-7K.

**Step 5 (run it)**
- 100-500 hands-on sessions × 2-10M on Opus 5.5 or Fable 5.1 = 0.2-5B, about $0.3K-20K.

**Step 6 (match behavior)**
- 500-3,000 failure clusters × (triage 1-3M + fixer 1-4M + reviewers 1-4M) = 1.5-33B, about $1K-40K.
- Plus judge compute: about 30-90 min per full run on this Mac.

**Total**
- About 15-140B processed tokens, i.e. order 10^10 to 10^11, mostly cache reads.
- About $10K-200K at API list prices, with the middle of the band around $30K-60K.
- Most of the multiplier is the review topology (about 2.5-3x the implementer alone) and the per-turn context re-reads.
- If the developer uses a subscription instead of the API, rate limits replace dollars as the constraint.

**Throughput**
- Step 3 takes about 2 weeks of continuous running at 40-80 concurrent agents. Each unit's pipeline takes about 20-60 min.
- At the concurrency this survey actually showed (43 agents), expect about 3-6 weeks.
- The Mac is not the limit in Step 3, because there is no compiler in the loop. It is the limit in Steps 4-6: one cargo daemon, 24 GiB of RAM for large checks and 2-4 judge instances, and 52 GiB of free disk, below an assumed 20-60 GB Rust target directory plus the 6.9 GB C++ build plus judge data directories.

**Wall clock and developer attention per step**

| Step | Wall | Attention |
|---|---|---|
| Decisions | 1-2 wk | 10-20 h |
| Judge (00b) | 3-6 wk | 30-60 h |
| Step 1 | 8-20 wk | 140-340 h |

| Step 3 | 2-6 wk | 20-40 h |
| Step 4 | 2-6 wk | 20-60 h |
| Step 5 | 3-10 wk | 80-250 h |

Several steps overlap, so the calendar total is about 6-18 months, with about 400-1,100 hours of attention.
positions.model_plan:
The largest model goes where an error replicates everywhere; the mid tier does the volume work. Chosen tiers become the [model] placeholders of prompts 01-06.

**Design document, rulebook amendments and the hand-built core crates: claude-fable-5-1** (effort high or xhigh).
One-time work, and every mistake in the ownership, error or IR design repeats across about 4,000 units. Its $0.25 cache-read price keeps long read-heavy design sessions affordable.

**00b judge building:**
- Corpus generation and scenario scripts: claude-sonnet-5.
- The two adversarial reviewers who check that no rewrite weakened an assertion: claude-opus-5-5 at effort high. A weak judge misleads every later step.

**01 dependency map:**
- claude-sonnet-5 adapts scripts/depmap_c.py.
- [reviewer model] = claude-opus-5-5. The misses here are subtle: forwarders, unity-hidden includes, declarations and code in different directories.

**02 gap inventory:**
- Classifiers: claude-opus-5-5 for ownership and lifetime rows; claude-sonnet-5 for mechanical families (ATOMIC_* retyping, error-convention rows).
- [reviewer model] = claude-opus-5-5.

**03 stress test and 04 translation:**
- [implementer model] = claude-sonnet-5 for most units.
- Promote to claude-opus-5-5 for the redesign-adjacent groups: sql-resolver-expr, sql-resolver-dml, sql-rewrite, sql-optimizer, storage-tablet-meta-ls, storage-tx-lock, storage-access-memtable, share-schema. There, pointer identity and ownership mistakes change behavior quietly.
- [reviewer model] = claude-opus-5-5. The gap is complex, and the reviewers are where catches come from.
- Fixers ride claude-sonnet-5.

**05 survey build:**
- [fixer model] = claude-sonnet-5; the compiler is the real referee.
- [reviewer model] = claude-opus-5-5.
- claude-haiku-4-5 only for mechanical queue work: bucketing errors by crate and code, and checking the TODO(port) trailer counts. Its 200K context is too small for translation units with context.

**Step 5 bootstrap debugging:** claude-opus-5-5 by default, and claude-fable-5-1 for the hardest sessions. Hands-on, few sessions, expensive mistakes.

**06 post-parity:** [reviewer model] = claude-opus-5-5.

**Do not use claude-opus-5.** At $5/$25 it costs more than claude-opus-5-5 at $4/$20 in the same tier.

**Settings:** claude-opus-5-5 defaults to effort medium, so set effort explicitly (high for reviewers, medium for implementers). Log every subagent's model in migration/cost-log.tsv.

verdict.single_fact:
How much of seekdb's hand-written code the 272-case judge actually executes: measured function coverage per unit group.

This decides whether "build the judge first" is a few weeks of work or a project comparable in cost to the port. Text matching gives only lower bounds (207 of 527 expressions, 44 of 89 resolvers, 9 of 34 rewrite rules), and nothing in the repo records a coverage run.

If the core-path groups (sql-expr, sql-operators, sql-optimizer, sql-rewrite, the sql-resolver-* groups, the storage-* groups, storage-tx-lock) show roughly 60% or more of their functions executed, the verdict stays "migrate later" with a bounded judge phase.

If they show under roughly 30%, the verdict becomes "don't migrate the whole of seekdb": harden the C++ and keep only chosen pieces in Rust. Most translated code would then ship unjudged, or the judge would cost as much as the translation.

Both thresholds are my assumptions.
verdict.how_to_check_in_a_day:
In a scratch worktree, never in migrate-to-rust's build_release:
1. Re-enable source-based coverage: remove the FATAL_ERROR guard at CMakeLists.txt:147 (added by 4cb6fb268), or pass -fprofile-instr-generate -fcoverage-mapping -DWITH_COVERAGE. src/observer/main.cpp:19 already sets the profraw file name.
2. Build. The clean build is 314 s uninstrumented, so budget 10-20 min.
3. Add the one-line --nodaemon call to .github/script/seekdb/mysqltest_for_seekdb.py prepare_instance.
4. Run the 272 configured cases (about 30-60 min instrumented) to produce <base_dir>/seekdb.profraw.
5. Run `llvm-profdata merge`, then `llvm-cov report --show-functions` against the seekdb binary.
6. Map the covered functions to the 52 unit groups from the ledger with a short script.
Total: about 3-5 hours, including one retry.

decisions_for_human.question: Which platforms must the Rust seekdb support?
options: Linux x86_64 + macOS arm64 only
Also Windows x64 and Android arm64
Also wasm32-unknown-emscripten (the shipped browser engine on feature/webassembly-shell)
decisions_for_human.recommendation: Linux x86_64 + macOS arm64 only for the port. Treat wasm, Windows and Android as later follow-ups, and put only the cheap wasm rules into the design doc now: u64 for every persisted field, no 128-bit atomics, network code behind cargo features.
decisions_for_human.why:
Each extra platform is another referee on every round.
- wasm needs nightly-2026-09-07 with -Zbuild-std, a patched std sysroot for thread-local destructors and panic=abort. It pins every kept C++ island to Emscripten, and it has no stack switching for 1,138 SMART_CALL sites.
- Windows and Android default to obmalloc with no malloc hook, so the abort-on-OOM policy would turn recoverable errors into process aborts there.
- No CI covers any platform except Linux.

decisions_for_human.question: Must the Rust build open existing C++ data directories?
options: No: bump DATA_CURRENT_VERSION and provide a tested logical export/import
Yes: byte-compatible with v1.4.0 or a named commit
decisions_for_human.recommendation: No. Bump the version, ship a round-trip-tested export from the C++ v1.4.0 binary into the Rust build, fix the missing-version-file hole, and move the version check ahead of the meta.db open.

decisions_for_human.question: Which embedded API is the product the port must keep?
options: seekdb-bindings' out-of-process driver (24 functions, spawns `seekdb --embedded --nodaemon`, MySQL protocol over run/sql.sock)
origin/feat/embedded-mode's in-process C ABI (93 functions, built on ObInnerSQLConnection and 40 internal headers)
decisions_for_human.recommendation: Settle it before Step 1. For the port, prefer the out-of-process contract. The 12 bindings tests and 7 seekdb-async tests already judge it unchanged, and it adds no second ABI to re-provide.
decisions_for_human.why: If the 197-commit feat/embedded-mode branch lands first, the port must also re-provide an in-process ABI over whatever replaces ObInnerSQLConnection. That is a second public surface, judged by 61 C++ cases and 6 language suites.

decisions_for_human.question: How does the C++ tree stay in step during the port?
options: Freeze at a named commit and stop taking upstream changes
Freeze, then replay upstream PRs at batch gates (about 8K ordinary lines a month, mostly src/sql/optimizer and src/sql/rewrite)
Keep developing C++ normally and chase it
decisions_for_human.recommendation: Freeze at a named commit after deciding the fate of feature/plugin (its Rust plugin runtime sets FFI and crate conventions), feat/embedded-mode, feature/webassembly-shell and feature/rust. Replay only correctness fixes, per PR, at batch gates.
decisions_for_human.why: Last 30 days: 32 ordinary src commits (+3,895/-3,944 lines) plus 3 bulk cuts removing 80,040 lines, and 34 branches were active. Chasing the tree means the reviewers' baseline moves under them. release/1.4.0 also still needs C++ fixes.

decisions_for_human.question: What happens when memory runs out?
options: Abort on OOM, plus typed budget checks at the 8 named owners and the logical -4013 errors
Fallible allocation everywhere (try_reserve and custom collections at about 4,700 sites)
decisions_for_human.recommendation: Abort plus named budgets, as rust/sql-nio already does.
decisions_for_human.why: In the default jemalloc build, about 40 of the 4,737 `ret = OB_ALLOCATE_MEMORY_FAILED` sites guard a failure that can happen. Allocation-failure injection works only on obmalloc, and no test expects -4013. Carrying the rest over costs per-unit tokens and reviewer attention for dead paths.

decisions_for_human.question: How strict is the judge's comparison?
options: Exact text, as today
Mask EST.ROWS/EST.TIME in the 40 plan files, and sort rows of unordered SELECTs per case
Normalize broadly (plans, warnings, order)
decisions_for_human.recommendation: Exact text by default, with the cost mask and row sorting as opt-in switches validated on C++ against C++ first. Keep the cost model and SORT algorithms structure-preserved so the switches are rarely needed.
decisions_for_human.why: Loose comparison hides regressions. Strict comparison floods Step 6 triage with false failures from float, tie and scan order. Per the kit, a referee that fails everything is usually broken, and each false failure costs about 1-3M tokens to triage.

decisions_for_human.question: Which pieces stay in C++ for good?
options: vsag, S2, share/geo with boost.geometry, ICU regex, and the bison parser
The same minus the parser (port the grammar to a Rust LR generator)
Rewrite GIS on georust too
decisions_for_human.recommendation: Keep all five for the first port, and revisit the parser and ICU after parity.
decisions_for_human.why: The GIS boundary alone needs about 76-140 entry points plus datum-free C++ kernels carved out of 14.9K lines of ST_ expression code, and 42 geometry suites pin boost numerics and error codes. The parser's grammar is 18,723 lines with C actions and a longjmp error path, and a replacement must reproduce the fast parser's constant counts or plan caching quietly stops.

decisions_for_human.question: How is the spend paid and capped?
options: API with prompt caching and a per-gate budget in migration/cost-log.tsv
A subscription, where rate limits rather than dollars set the pace
decisions_for_human.recommendation: API with caching for the fan-out, with a hard budget per gate. Accept a band of about $10K-200K only after the Phase A-B pilot confirms per-unit token use.
decisions_for_human.why: Most of the multiplier comes from the review topology and per-turn context re-reads. The band is wide (10-100x in tokens) until real per-unit numbers exist.

decisions_for_human.question: Does the local machine need to grow?
options: Keep the M4 Pro as it is (52 GiB free disk, 24 GiB RAM)
Free about 150 GB or add an external SSD; optionally rent a Linux box for nightly judge runs
decisions_for_human.recommendation: Free or add disk before Step 4, and consider a Linux runner for nightly judge runs, since the recorded .result files come from Linux CI.
decisions_for_human.why: A Rust target directory for about 2.5M lines is assumed to need 20-60 GB next to the 6.9 GB C++ build and judge data directories. RAM limits the daemon to 2-4 large crate checks and 2-4 judge instances at a time.

risks: The first end-to-end SQL signal from the Rust tree arrives only after about 90% of the code is translated and compiling. Bootstrap needs inner-table schema loading through inner SQL, the generated inner tables and the PL resolvers for system packages, and init.sql needs PL, set_tp and virtual tables. Until then only reviewers, the compiler and library-level parity tests judge the work, so design mistakes surface late.

The developer's attention peaks in Steps 5-6 (an estimated 160-500 hours), when one person must debug a 2M-line system at boot with no partial signal. Every hour spent there delays the whole calendar.

Judge reach may be low: 207 of 527 expressions, 44 of 89 resolvers and 9 of 34 rewrite rules by text match. Translated code the judge never executes can pass Step 6 unverified. The unit tests that could have covered it were deleted in 45cbbe9e1.

Exact-text comparison can swamp triage with false failures: 568 cost-bearing plan tables, SORT tie order, storage scan order behind about 7,500 unordered SELECTs, and inserted casts in 4,005 output lines. The runner also retries each failing case 3 times and shares one instance per slice, so flakiness and order dependence are hidden today.

Replacing pointer identity with ExprId (about 580 find_item/set-helper lines, the ADJUST_SHARED_EXPR pass) can change which expressions count as the same object and quietly change plans. Only 40 plan-pinned cases would notice.

Check-rate uncertainty is 5-10x (500-5,000 lines/s per core). Edits to foundation crates re-check every downstream crate (2-4 min central, up to 15-30 min). Cargo's build-directory lock serializes concurrent checks, and 52 GiB of free disk is below the assumed Rust target size. Any of these can double the Step 4 calendar.

The current rust/Cargo.toml release profile (codegen-units=1, lto=thin) turns large crates into hour-long builds (Databend 30m37s for one ~181K-line crate). rust/Cargo.lock is gitignored and cmake/Rust.cmake calls cargo without --locked, so builds are not reproducible across worktrees.

The tree is a moving target: about 8K ordinary lines a month plus ongoing cuts. There are 34 active branches, including feature/plugin, whose 34.6K Rust lines set competing FFI and crate conventions, and feature/webassembly-shell, which conflicts with HEAD in 9 sql-nio files. release/1.4.0 still needs C++ fixes.

The cost band is wide (about $10K-200K, 10^10-10^11 processed tokens) and depends on cache hit rate and on rate limits that were not measured. At the concurrency this survey showed, Step 3 alone takes 3-6 weeks of continuous running.

Redesign mistakes replicate. An error in the arena, error-type or context design repeats across about 4,000 units. The kit's bakeoff is invalid for a redesign, and a disposable run costs a meaningful share of Step 3.

The payoff cannot be measured with today's tools. Memory bugs are found by internal Sanity builds and sqlqa suites that are not in the repo, and the public judge caught none of the cited crashes. A safer Rust core would have to be proven with new stress tooling.

There is no performance judge (only a prose sysbench line of about 43.7k QPS at d65d43b and one wasm timing JSON). The plan leans on compiler auto-vectorization of 16-row bitmap loops, and hand-tuned hazard-pointer and SIMD code becomes unsafe Rust. A slower Rust engine could pass every functional test.

The C++ islands keep OpenSSL (S2, curl and gRPC need it), the malloc hook (island allocations are charged through it) and the C++ exception boundary, where every extern "C" entry needs its own catch. On wasm they would also pin the Emscripten JS exception model.

The report is written to /Users/colin/.claude/jobs/39d4f781/tmp/report/feasibility-draft.md (1,317 lines). It follows prompts/00-feasibility.md, then adds "Where the analysts disagree" and "Decisions for the developer" after the verdict. The cost-log line was not appended, because the draft was the only file I was allowed to write. The report gives the row for the orchestrator to append: `0	2026-09-24T06:37Z	117	8920000	43	unknown`.

**Verdict: migrate later.** Start now on the work that pays off either way:
- the differential judge (prompts/00b-judge-setup.md) on this Mac;
- the coverage run and the performance baselines;
- measuring the `cargo check` rate;
- the decisions.

Step 1 starts only after the judge is validated and a disposable run of the redesigned core passes.

**The three calls:**
- **Structure or redesign: redesign.** The ownership core (about 300K lines at the narrowest, up to about 600K) is redesigned by hand. The other 2,600-3,100 stems are translated file by file against it, keeping every function that produces text the judge compares. vsag, S2, share/geo with boost.geometry, ICU regex and the bison parser stay in C++.
- **Verification cost: cheap per unit, expensive per behavior.**
  - A crate check fits in the loop only if seekdb becomes 20-40 acyclic crates of at most about 100-180K lines, and `codegen-units=1` is dropped.
  - Each judge pass costs about 30 minutes on this Mac.
  - Measured baseline: 314 s clean C++ build, 9-37 s per edit.
- **Tests: the 272 mysqltest cases survive, but they are not enough to judge the migration.**
  - Every run first has to pass an init.sql entry gate.
  - The runner retries each failing case up to 4 times on a shared instance.
  - There are 0 restart, 0 binary-protocol and 0 out-of-memory cases.
  - The judge has to be built before Step 1.

**Cost:**
- Tokens: about 3-30B as counted by this survey's harness counter, or about 10-140B counting cache re-reads.
- Money: roughly $10K-$300K at list prices, most likely tens of thousands of dollars.
- Time: about 12-24 months of calendar and about 600-2,800 hours of the developer's attention. The core build is what swings the total.

**The fact that would change the verdict:** how much of the code to be redesigned the 272 cases actually execute, measured by function coverage over two identical runs.
- About 60% or more shrinks "later" to the judge-and-pilot phase.
- Under about a third means don't migrate the whole of seekdb.
- It can be checked in one day with a coverage build in a scratch worktree.

**Decisions for the developer:**
1. Is the Rust seekdb meant for upstream oceanbase/seekdb, or for your fork?
2. How does Rust replace the C++?
3. Must the Rust build open data directories written by the C++ build?
4. Which platforms must the first Rust release support?
5. Which embedding model is the product?
6. What happens when an allocation fails?
7. Which pieces stay C++ for good?
8. Where may `unsafe` code appear?
9. How exact must the judge's comparison be?
10. How does the server stop during the port?
11. How does the port keep up with the moving C++ tree?
12. What happens to the parallel branches before the design freezes?
13. Which model tier runs each phase?
14. How is the spend paid for and capped?
15. Does the machine need to grow?

issues.section: 9. Verdict: How to check it in under a day

issues.evidence: src/observer/main.cpp (the WITH_COVERAGE block) calls `__llvm_profile_set_filename("<base_dir>/seekdb%c.profraw")` from a constructor, so counters go into the base dir. In .github/script/seekdb/mysqltest_for_seekdb.py, `prepare_instance` (157-158) calls `destroy_instance` first. `prepare_instance` runs again after every failing case (516-518), and the `finally:` block after the loop calls `destroy_instance` once more. sdb.py `command_destroy` runs `shutil.rmtree(str(base_dir))` (sdb.py:488). With MAX_CASE_RETRIES=0, each failing case wipes the counters collected so far in that slice, and the end of every slice wipes the rest.
issues.fix: Add to step 1: patch the runner to copy `<base_dir>/seekdb*.profraw` into `--work-dir` before every `destroy_instance`, including the one in `finally`. The alternative is to patch main.cpp to write outside the base dir; LLVM_PROFILE_FILE is not a way out, because the constructor's API call wins. reviews.overall: I spot-checked about 70 claims against evidence-full.md and the code (read-only), weighted toward the three calls, the cost section and the verdict. Most of them reproduce exactly: the section 2 commit hashes and paths; the Call 1 counts (2,498/6,644 ObIAllocator files, 2,741 placement-new lines, 5,938 raw-pointer fields, 1,222 server_service lines over 122 types, ob_tablet_scan.h:442-448, the 271/100, 382/156 and 427/131 link cycles); the bit-exact list (568 plan tables, 4,005 output lines, 3,598 rowset=, 770,711/912,659, 1,546 errno entries, 12 set_tp lines, 322 tracepoint definitions, 169 `lib::ob_sort` lines); the build baseline (314 s, 8/306 s, 9 s, 37 s = 32 + 3.5 + 1.2, 7 s, 17 s, 193 MB); CI (223 s, 556 + 258 s, slice medians summing to 29.4 min); the runner lines (19, 52-74, 157-194, 502); sdb.py:127-128; ob_signal_handle.cpp:129-134; CMakeLists.txt:147; the data-version citations; 186 `unsafe` (70 + 53); rust-toolchain 1.98.1; the release profile; 716 upstream commits with 2 by the developer; model prices; and most token arithmetic. I also confirmed from sibling repos: 12 bindings gtests, 7 tokio tests, 68 Playwright tests (3 + 65 scenarios), 53 wasm .cpp tests and about 41 add_test lines on the wasm branch. The verdict \"migrate later\", building the judge first, and the three committed lines are supported. The problems cluster in three places. First, the verdict section: the under-a-day coverage check deletes its own profraw files because the runner rmtree's the base dir; the Step 1 gate depends on a Step 2 result; and the \"identical runs\" rule ignores known flaky cases. Second, the cost and duration arithmetic: the processed column is not x3-7, the calendar total is below the sum of the table, and the Step 3 wall-clock product does not give 2-8 weeks. reviews.overall: Every section the rubric requires is present. The six steps are restated one line each. The case for leaving rests on specific commits from this repo. Each of the three calls ends in a committed line with file paths. Call 2 has the measured baseline and a stated scaling assumption. Call 3 counts public-surface against internal tests and treats the judge as a gate, with 17 parity scenarios to seed 00b. Every step names its prompt and shows units times a per-unit estimate. Cost is given in bands with the drivers shown. Wall clock and attention are given per step in minutes, and the model plan gives a tier and a reason for each phase. The problems are correctness and consistency, not missing pieces. One blocker: the under-a-day check for the deciding fact would delete its own coverage files, because main.cpp:19 writes seekdb.profraw inside the base dir and the runner removes the base dir before every start, after every failed case and at the end of every slice (sdb.py:488, mysqltest_for_seekdb.py:158/493/520/533). The majors: (1) sections 10 and 11 sit between the Verdict and the closing, against the rubric's order; (2) a 'later' verdict starts 00b, whose prerequisite is a signed-off 'migrate', and the verdict never literally names 'build the judge first'; (3) the core build, the largest phase, sits outside the kit with no prompt, queue or gate, and Step 2 narrows the README's disposable full runs without saying what that loses; (4) three pieces of arithmetic do not add up: Step 3 wall clock, the processed-token column against its own x3-7 multiplier, and the calendar total against the per-step table; (5) the closing says one build and no edits, but six build commands ran, two after file edits; (6) the directory list for the deciding fact does not match the draft's definition of the core, and the 'don't' branch rests on an unquantified claim; (7) the decisions are not ordered by what the next action needs, since Decisions 9 and 13 must be made before 00b but are listed late and left out of the verdict's conditions. With the check repaired, the sections reordered and the numbers recomputed, the report would meet the rubric. Its main conclusions (redesign the ownership core, keep five C++ pieces, build the judge first, the verdict leaning 'later') are well supported by the evidence.

(c) The narrow 299K core leaves out the DAG scheduler's raw parent/child graph, the IO manager's hand-kept double reference counts, the share/cache hazard-version reclamation, the thread pools (where 40fcfa901 and 328253969 lived), lib/utility and share/rc. The code that must be redesigned or rewritten against new signatures is therefore nearer 0.8-1M lines than 300K.
issues.evidence: Evidence-brief sql-optimizer verifier (488 ObRawExpr*& parameters, 18,618 OB_FAIL lines, about 580 find_item call lines; 'Any ExprId design has to reproduce these equality semantics exactly, or plans change'); sql-engine verifier (66/156; 183 expression files). ParseNode: 206 files, 2,610 references (draft :278). Draft :198-207 (foundation 57,762 lines), :232, :247-256, :603. Runtime area: DAG scheduler 8,594 lines, IO 15,050, share/cache 8,356; the verifier puts the runtime near 170K hand-written lines. Idioms verifier: foundation about 91.8K lines, plus lib/rc and share/rc.
issues.fix: Choose one. (i) Specify an IR id design that mirrors pointer semantics one for one (one id per allocation, in-place edits keep the id, new ids only where ObRawExprCopier makes copies) and a Rust mirror of ParseNode, so the optimizer, rewrite and resolvers really keep their structure. This also keeps upstream fixes replayable (Decision 11). (ii) State in the committed line that about 0.8-1M lines are rewritten against new APIs, add the runtime pieces to the core table, and treat those groups as subsystem units with the stronger implementer tier and a higher per-unit token band.

issues.section: 6. Step 2 (disposable run) and Decision 2 (switch condition)
issues.problem: The disposable run's pass criterion cannot be met by the path it builds, so the switch to (b) will fire because the run is incomplete, not because the design is wrong. The path covers 'simple SELECT, INSERT and CREATE TABLE' on memtable-only storage, but condition 4 requires passing 'the plain-SQL cases under the reduced init'. Those 130 cases include joins (the draft's own example is t/join_basic.test), and exact-text output needs the expression printer, casts, type deduction and error text. CREATE TABLE alone reaches ObDDLService, the schema service and the build-time inner-table schema, which must first be retargeted to Rust. Path (b) is described but has no row in section 7, even though the draft's own switch condition makes it the likely path.
issues.evidence: Draft :603, :610, :855, :1021, :1026-1030. src/rootserver/ob_ddl_service.cpp is 23,564 lines (ledger oversize list). The inner-table schema is 103,354 lines in 51 files generated at build time (build-platforms area). Resolver reach: CreatePackage and CreatePackageBody run at startup.
issues.fix: Make the pass criterion a small, named statement list, for example 20-50 single-table statements taken from the plain-SQL cases and diffed against the C++ reference under the reduced init. Keep the 130 cases as a later core-build gate. Add a costed section 7 row for path (b).

issues.section: 6. Step 2 (replacement for the bakeoff)
issues.problem: This departs from the kit. For redesigns the README replaces the bakeoff with 'disposable full runs — run the whole migration cheaply, review what came out, fix the rules, throw the run away'. The draft uses a narrow end-to-end path instead. A narrow path cannot show the design's riskiest claims: that 20-40 crates form an acyclic graph over the whole tree, and that the typed-ID IR survives the find_item call sites and the 34 rewrite rules.
issues.evidence: README, 'If you're redesigning'. Draft :599-610. Unit-ledger verifier: one include cycle of 110 directories and 4,108 files; 42 of 52 unit groups form one cycle. Build-platforms verifier: link-level pairs sql<->storage 271/100, pl<->sql 382/156, observer<->sql 427/131.
issues.fix: Add a cheap full pass against the draft design: one Sonnet 5 implementer run per unit, no reviewers, no compiler, then one survey cargo check to count cross-crate cycle and API errors. About 3,000-3,500 units x 1 run x 0.15-0.6M ≈ 0.45-2.1B harness-counted tokens, which fits inside the draft's Step 2 band (0.09-2.4B). Otherwise label the narrow path as a deviation and say what it cannot show.

issues.section: 3. What must stay the same, to the bit, vs What the redesigned core looks like; Decision 9
issues.problem: The draft requires bit-exact EST.ROWS while redesigning the storage that produces it. EST.ROWS comes partly from storage estimation over sstable and macro-block metadata and over memtable-versus-sstable state. The draft redesigns the sstable formats and the memtable, and different block sizes, rows per block or freeze timing change EST.ROWS in the 568 plan tables. rowset= comes from ObCodeGenerator::detect_batch_size, inside the redesigned code generator. The committed line lists ob_opt_est_cost_model.cpp as bit-exact, but the numbers it prints depend on inputs the plan changes.
issues.evidence: Draft :157-161, :212, :244, :296. Judge-reach verifier: ob_access_path_estimation.cpp:165 and :569-669 call src/storage/access/ob_table_estimator.cpp and ob_index_sstable_estimator.cpp. Tests force merges through index_quick_major.inc and wait_daily_merge.inc. rowset= appears on 3,598 lines (3,035 + 563), set by detect_batch_size.
issues.fix: Decide explicitly and say which. Either keep the estimator inputs identical (block sizes, rows per micro and macro block, freeze thresholds) as a named design constraint, or declare EST.ROWS, EST.TIME and rowset= masks for the 40 plan-bearing files in advance under Decision 9(b) and take them off the bit-exact list.

issues.section: 3. Where a faithful translation still changes behavior silently, item 3; 5. Build the judge first, item 2
issues.problem: The differential judge compares a C++ reference built on this Mac with clang, which by default fuses a*b+c into one FMA instruction on arm64, against Rust, which never does. No build file sets -ffp-contract. The checked-in .result files come from Linux x86 CI, where baseline x86-64 has no FMA (only ob_sql_simd and ob_storage_simd get -mfma). So the Mac C++ reference can differ from both the Linux results and Rust in the last bit, cross a ceil() boundary in any of the 568 plan tables, and produce false Step 6 failures.
issues.evidence: Draft :182-186 (labeled an assumption). git grep for fp-contract across cmake/, bazel/, CMakeLists.txt, src/CMakeLists.txt and src/sql/CMakeLists.txt: 0 hits. src/sql/CMakeLists.txt:12-15 adds -mfma only for ob_sql_simd, and only on x86_64.
issues.fix: Build the pinned C++ reference with -ffp-contract=off for every judge run (00b item 2). Record in the design document that Rust uses mul_add only where the reference does. It costs little and removes a whole class of false failures.

issues.section: 3. The C++ that stays, behind a C ABI; 6. intro; Decision 2 (Why); Decision 7
issues.problem: The islands are not C-like seams. Keeping ObParser, ObFastParser, ObPLParser and share/geo in C++ keeps a C++ copy of the oblib allocator, ObString, charset, containers, logging and worker code alive in the Rust binary. That is the same 'two foundations living side by side' cost the draft counts against option (b). ob_fast_parser.h even includes a plan-cache header.
issues.evidence: A read-only include-closure count over git-tracked files (include roots src, src/oblib, src/query/api, src/data_plane/api): ob_fast_parser.cpp reaches 362 files / 137,510 lines (207 in src/oblib/lib, 31 in src/share/schema); ob_parser.cpp 246 / 95,651 (185 in oblib/lib); share/geo/ob_geo_func_register.h 203 / 73,511 (148 in oblib/lib); ob_s2adapter.cpp 185 / 72,220. ob_fast_parser.h includes lib/allocator/ob_allocator.h, lib/charset/ob_charset.h and sql/plan_cache/ob_plan_cache_struct.h; ob_fast_parser.cpp includes lib/worker.h. Draft :517, :923, :1030.
issues.fix: Keep only the parser's C core (the bison/flex output, sql_parser_base.c, parse_node.c). Port ObFastParser (2.5K lines) to Rust, checked by the plan-cache hit differential already in 00b item 6. For share/geo and S2, size the C++ oblib subset each island needs at link level and list it as kept C++, with its build, allocator hook and a rule that charset behavior matches. Add a cost row for the island shims. Otherwise drop the 'two foundations' argument against (b).

issues.section: Decision 6 (allocation failure), with Decision 4 (platforms)
issues.problem: Option (c) is not really a separate option. Whether the core uses infallible Vec and Box or try_reserve-style collections is fixed across the whole workspace when the core is written, so a 'separate stated policy for Windows and Android' cannot be added later without rewriting those paths. wasm, which Decision 4 makes the next platform with its rules in force from day one, has a 2 GiB heap that is never returned. Out-of-memory is reachable there, and abort kills the in-browser database. The list of budget owners also misses the micro block cache's 4 GB FIFO and its 3-try sleep loop.
issues.evidence: Draft :1092-1115 and :1061-1076 (wasm: 2 GiB never returned; panic=abort for the whole program). OOM verifier (d): Windows x64, Android arm64 and Bazel non-sanity builds default to obmalloc with no malloc hook, and Windows has no overcommit. OOM verifier (c): ob_micro_block_cache.cpp:396-402 and :1115-1118.
issues.fix: Decide the per-platform behavior now. Either state that Windows, Android and wasm accept abort on allocation failure and what the user sees, or choose fallible collections in the named budget owners and in paths whose size a client controls, and apply that rule on every platform. Add the micro block cache FIFO to the budget-owner list.

issues.section: 6. Step 2 (For the leaves ... run 03 as written)
issues.problem: The bakeoff is still invalid for the leaves. In prompt 03, Translator B gets only the source files and must never see the rulebook. Here the rulebook is the design document plus the frozen core API, so B would port the leaves against an API it invents, and the diff would again measure the redesign. That is why the README says the bakeoff breaks for redesigns.
issues.evidence: prompts/03-stress-test.md ('only valid for structure-preserving migrations'; 'B must never see the rulebook or learn it exists'). README 'If you're redesigning'. Draft :292, :612-621.
issues.fix: For the leaves, run only the pilot half of 03: the production pipeline, graded on rulebook adherence. Or give B the core crates as ordinary dependencies (public API docs only, never the rulebook) and name this as a change to prompt 03.

issues.section: Decision 1, Decision 11, 9. go-conditions, 7. Cost and duration
issues.problem: Upstream alignment and replay are neither a go-condition nor costed. The developer has 2 of 716 upstream commits. Upstream changes about 8K ordinary lines a month, concentrated in src/sql/optimizer and src/sql/rewrite, which the draft redesigns and says cannot be replayed mechanically. Over a 12-24-month port that is roughly 100-200K lines. Each replay window also moves the pinned C++ reference, so the judge must be re-recorded under the reduced init and validated again (N/N twice, plus mutations). None of this is in section 7, and the verdict does not depend on the answer to Decision 1.
issues.evidence: Draft :1000-1008, :1171-1183, :796. Moving-target area: 30 days = 32 ordinary commits, +3,895/-3,944 lines; 9-11 of 16 ordinary src/sql commits in optimizer or rewrite, all by one author; mysql_test went from 600 cases to 283 in six months; 24 commits re-recorded plan rows in a year.
issues.fix: Make the answer to Decision 1 a go-condition. Add a replay row to section 7 (per window: diff the upstream tree, port the fixes, re-record the C++ reference, validate the judge again), with token and attention bands. If upstream says no, say what the fork is for once it is 12-24 months behind.

issues.section: 6. Step 6 referee price; 7. Machine time
issues.problem: The Step 6 inner-loop price (3-12 min for 'an incremental build plus the failing cases') conflicts with section 4's release build of 15-45 min. Debug builds cannot stand in: integer overflow panics in debug (Call 1, item 4), and unoptimized Rust is far too slow to run the 272 cases in anything like 30 min. How long an optimized incremental rebuild and link takes after a foundation-crate edit is not measured. At 10-30 min per build, the 15-1,200 machine-hours become roughly 50-3,600, which on one Mac can exceed the 2-6-month Step 6 window.
issues.fix: Define a judge build profile (opt-level 1-2, overflow checks as in release, many codegen units, no LTO, incremental on). Have the Step 2 pilot measure its incremental rebuild and link time. Restate Step 6 machine time from that measurement and say whether Step 6 is limited by the one Mac.

issues.section: Decision 4; 5. Is it enough to judge (Platform); Decision 15
issues.problem: No Linux gate exists. Decision 4 has the first release support Linux x86_64 and macOS arm64, but the differential judge runs only on this Mac against a C++ reference recorded on the Mac. CI runs only on OceanBase-internal Linux runners, and Decision 15 makes a Linux box optional. Linux parity therefore has no done-gate, even though the .result files were recorded on Linux x86 and libc++ and libstdc++ already order sort ties differently.
issues.evidence: Draft :374 (CI on OceanBase-internal Linux runners only), :434, :1059-1061, :1157, :1235.
issues.fix: Either require a Linux x86_64 runner before Step 6 and run the done-gate on both platforms, or make the first release macOS-only and say so in Decision 4.

issues.section: Decision 2, option (d)
issues.problem: Option (d) is rejected on an unlabeled assertion. 'A literal port of this compiles only as unsafe Rust throughout' is not a count. (d) also has the properties the draft values in (b): a Rust binary running under the unchanged judge early, a valid bakeoff, the file-level units the kit is built for, upstream fixes that replay mechanically, and a redesign done later under a passing judge. Its real costs are not weighed either: Rust has no inheritance for 4,364 derived classes, and there are 7,275 template heads, placement new, and serialized unions of function pointers.
issues.evidence: Draft :151, :1018-1033. Unit-ledger surveyor: 'supports structure-preserving translation at the stem level for most of the code'. Moving-target verifier: keeping the file and function layout is 'the right call while the C++ tree is still moving'. Idioms and unit-ledger verifiers: ObIAllocator in about 38% of files; 4,364 derived classes; 17,225 lines containing 'virtual'.
issues.fix: Add a costed comparison of (d) against (a) and (b): units x review topology, time to the first judge signal, and the rework afterwards. Or label the 'unsafe throughout' claim an assumption and name the measurement that would settle it, for example the unsafe count per 1K lines in a 3-file structure-preserving pilot.

issues.section: 3. What the redesigned core looks like (Statement IR); Decision 4
issues.problem: 'Explicit work stacks instead of SMART_CALL' at 1,138 sites rewrites recursive algorithms in the resolvers, rewrite rules, optimizer and printer, which contradicts 'keeps its structure'. On native targets a stack-growing crate such as stacker does what SMART_CALL does, so the rewrite is only needed for wasm.
issues.evidence: Draft :192, :233, :1065, :1073. (That stacker behaves this way, and fails on wasm, is an assumption to check.)
issues.fix: Use stack growth on native targets. On wasm, use a recursion depth limit that returns today's error (OB_SIZE_OVERFLOW). Record both as one rulebook entry.

issues.section: 11. Decisions (missing toolchain decision)
issues.problem: There is no decision on stable versus nightly Rust, although three choices pull in different directions. wasm needs nightly-2026-09-07 with -Zbuild-std and a private std patch. The referee price assumes stable, with one thread per crate because -Zthreads is nightly-only. Arena-aware fallible collections need allocator_api (unstable) or allocator-api2.
issues.evidence: Draft :335, :1072. rust/rust-toolchain.toml pins channel '1.98.1'. Idioms verifier, point (3).
issues.fix: Add a decision: pinned stable for native builds with wasm on its own nightly, plus rules for code that must compile on both; or one pinned nightly for everything, which enables -Zthreads, and then re-measure the per-crate check price.

issues.section: 5. Build the judge first, item 8, and parity scenario 6; Decision 3
issues.problem: Golden bytes for OB_UNIS, ObNumber and JSON binary are pinned in the judge, but Decision 3 drops byte compatibility and the core plan introduces new on-disk formats. A test-only FFI harness into C++ internals is also internal-bound under the kit's definition in 00b.
issues.evidence: Draft :244, :451, :478, :1038-1053. prompts/00b-judge-setup.md, step 1 (internal-bound tests are not judge material).
issues.fix: Split the list. Formats that are real contracts (the CRC32C algorithm, zstd frames, anything on the MySQL wire) stay in the judge. Persisted formats freed by the version bump move to differential tests of the value libraries, outside the judge.

issues.section: 6. Step 3 (Wall clock)
issues.problem: The multiplication shown does not give 2-8 weeks. 12,000 runs x 10 min / 80 concurrent ≈ 25 hours, and 15,000 x 30 min / 20 ≈ 16 days.
issues.evidence: Draft :656.
issues.fix: Show what accounts for the rest (28-35 batch gates with sign-off, token-per-minute rate limits), or restate the band as about 1 day to 2.5 weeks of running plus gate time.

issues.section: 7. Wall clock and active attention (Core build; Totals)
issues.problem: The core-build attention floor of 200 h is below every analyst's figure (the end-state analyst gave 400-1,200 h for 300K lines), with no reason given. The calendar total of 12-24 months is below the serial sum of the step table (about 9-31 months), and the draft does not say which steps overlap.
issues.evidence: Draft :785, :793, :940, :944, :981. Serial sum: low about 40 weeks, high about 133 weeks.
issues.fix: Use 400 h as the floor or explain the lower figure. List the overlaps that bring about 31 months down to 24, and mention the risk analyst's 1-2.5 years.

issues.section: 8. Model plan (04 implementers); Decision 13
issues.problem: The Opus 5.5 implementer groups include storage-tx-lock, storage-tablet-meta-ls, storage-access-memtable and sql-resolver-expr, which Call 1 puts in the hand-built core rather than in Step 3. Decision 13(c) is also rejected without a price: under the draft's own blend, an Opus 5.5 run costs about 1.7x a Sonnet 5 run ($1.2 vs $0.7 per million processed tokens). That is a small premium if the leaves really are rewrites against a new API.
issues.evidence: Draft :206, :754-756, :818, :1207-1216. claude-api skill shared/models.md:77 (Opus 5.5 cache reads $0.20).
issues.fix: Remove the core groups from the 04 list. Put a price on Decision 13(c), and reconsider it if the leaves turn out to be rewrites (issue on Call 1 scope).

issues.section: 9. Condition 5; 6. Before Step 1; Decision 15
issues.problem: Disk space is gated at three different points: 150 GB free before Step 1 (condition 5), in the pre-Step-1 list, and 'before Step 4' in Decision 15.
issues.fix: Pick one point and use it everywhere.

issues.section: 9. Start now; 6. Before Step 1 (00b scope and cost)
issues.problem: Running 00b before a 'migrate' verdict departs from the kit, whose prerequisite for 00b is a signed-off 'migrate' verdict. The draft's reason (the work pays off anyway) is fair, but the deviation is not named. The 00b band (0.04-0.55B tokens, 30-100 h) also looks thin for 12 harness tasks and 17 families. These include a C++ FFI golden-bytes harness, a generator that runs 527 expressions over a type matrix, fixing and building the bindings gtests on macOS, sysbench at three thread counts, and wasm wiring. The kit marks 00b as not yet tried in practice.
issues.evidence: prompts/00b-judge-setup.md, 'When' and the note that it was designed but not yet dogfooded. Draft :438-459, :524-539, :781.
issues.fix: Name the deviation. Widen the 00b band, or split 00b into a core set the verdict needs (differential mode, retries off, reduced init, coverage, restart) and later families.

issues.section: 5. Build the judge first; 6. Step 6 (keeping the C++ reference runnable)
issues.problem: The old code must stay runnable on this Mac for 12-24 months. But deps/3rd is downloaded at build time and not tracked, and the judge uses the prebuilt arm64 mysqltest and obclient from deps/3rd/u01. A change in the toolchain or the download mirror could break the reference partway through the port.
issues.evidence: Referee-price area: 'deps/ tracks only 29 files ... deps/3rd is copied or downloaded at build time'. Draft :447, :898.
issues.fix: In 00b, archive the pinned C++ build: the binary, deps/3rd, obclient and mysqltest, the toolchain version, and the recorded reference outputs. Check once that a clean rebuild from the archive works.

reviews.overall: Most of the draft's calls are backed by the evidence: redesign the ownership core, keep vsag and S2 in C++, build the judge first, bump the data version and provide export, and abort on out-of-memory in the jemalloc builds. The GIS and parser islands hold up on semantics, but they are not C-like seams: they keep 95-137K lines of C++ oblib headers alive in the Rust binary (see the islands issue). The plan built on these calls does not hold up yet. Two defects block it. First, the verdict gates Step 1 on a disposable run that needs Step 1's design document, so the plan cannot start as written. Second, the recipe for the deciding fact cannot measure anything, because the runner does `shutil.rmtree(base_dir)` on the directory that holds the profraw (sdb.py:488, mysqltest_for_seekdb.py:520 and 533-535). The reasoning has three further weaknesses. The verdict does not follow from section 2's own conclusion that the case does not justify the cost, and neither the chosen fact nor any go-condition bears on the payoff. The per-unit plan assumes file-by-file translation where the optimizer and engine verifiers describe rewriting every file against a new IR. The processed-token multiplier is below the minimum the draft's own per-run assumptions imply, so the top of the dollar band is likely two to three times low. The strategy also has open conflicts for one developer on one Mac. The disposable run's pass criterion needs most of the SQL stack, so the switch to option (b) will almost certainly fire. Bit-exact EST.ROWS conflicts with redesigned storage estimators. The C++ reference fuses FMA while Rust does not. There is no Linux gate. Upstream replay is neither costed nor gated. The kit's disposable full runs are replaced by a narrow path. Option (d) is dismissed without a cost comparison. "Migrate later" is defensible. As written, though, it is closer to "don't migrate the whole unless the payoff decision, the upstream answer and a fixed coverage check all come back well". The report should say so once the two blockers are fixed.

applied: Blocker (all three reviewers), coverage check: rewrote the under-a-day procedure (section 11) and 00b item 10. destroy_instance now runs `sdb.py stop` and copies <base_dir>/seekdb*.profraw into <work_dir>/profraw/ before `sdb.py destroy`; the reason is given (main.cpp:19-48 writes inside the base dir; the runner destroys it at lines 493/510/520/533-535; sdb.py:488 runs rmtree). Added: LLVM_PROFILE_FILE can't override the constructor; `-DWITH_COVERAGE=ON` goes before --make (build.sh:241-242); the full runner command with --seekdb/--obclient/--mysqltest/--base-dir/--work-dir/--port, with mkdir and the log inside the run dir; the passes run one after another; a one-case dry run (--slice-count 272) that confirms a .profraw survives; the matching clang-17 llvm-profdata/llvm-cov from deps/3rd devtools; and the parser is reworded as 'not counted' (src/sql/parser/CMakeLists.txt:56-59).

Circular gate (all three): kept the kit order. The Step 1 go-conditions are the judge validated, the Gate A+B decisions (with payoff and upstream answers), the base frozen and coverage at least about 60%. The Step 2a disposable-run results now gate the core build and the Step 3 fan-out. Section 6's order list, section 7's rows and Decision 10's switch point (end of Step 2a) are updated to match.

Flaky cases: two runs must now agree against a quarantine list named before the runs, seeded with the four SKILL.md:260-271 cases, with zero differences allowed outside the list. This applies in the 00b exit, 00b item 12, go-condition 1 and the single fact.

The Step 2a pilot logs both counters from the API usage objects. Decision 5's re-decide triggers now include the measured ratio and a dollar ceiling set on the bill's counter.

Also: #920 'probably fixed but not closed'; 65997991e split out as a logic bug; the 'where crashes were found' sentence limited to the checked commits, with fe79a0dd6/5aa611c00/1e4f589b8 sources; '9 of 16' src/sql commits; 'at most about 17-18 distinct fixes (about 24 commits); surveyor counted about 20'.
